From Service Account to System There are many occasions in penetration testing engagements that the penetration tester has managed to compromise a service like Apache, IIS, SQL, MySQL etc. but unfortunately this service is not running as local system or under a high\xc2 privileged account\xc2 but as network service. Apache Service running as Network Service The list of available tokens via Meterpeter in this case is limited only to\xc2 the Network Service as the Apache is running under this account. Meterpreter \xe2\x80\x93 Available Tokens However there is a technique which can be used that\xc2 tries to trick the \xe2\x80\x9cNT Authority\\System\xe2\x80\x9d\xc2 account\xc2 to negotiate and authenticate via NTLM locally so the token for the \xe2\x80\x9cNT Authority\\System\xe2\x80\x9d account would become available and therefore privilege escalation possible. This technique is called Rotten Potato and it was introduced in DerbyCon 2016\xc2 by Stephen Breen and Chris Mallz. Privilege Escalation \xe2\x80\x93 Rotten Potato Service Running as Administrator Alternatively if the service is running as high privileged user like administrator or if the service allows users to connect via Windows authentication (i.e. SQL Server allows that) then it is possible to escalate privilege by impersonating the token of the administrator account. Apache Service Running as Administrator This can be done through the Metasploit Framework\xc2 incognito extension or directly\xc2 through MWR Infosecurity tool\xc2 incognito. Metasploit \xe2\x80\x93 Token Impersonation Incognito \xe2\x80\x93 Listing the available tokens PowerSploit Manipulation of system tokens can be done also through PowerSploit as Joseph Bialek inspired by the tool incognito wrote a PowerShell script which can perform the same activities.
